items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.content: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0 , when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible . Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. ( The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe , their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic. ” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers . “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies . And what we built has really resonated with them.” After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees. ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native. ” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? items.content: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search. Tags: gemini , llm , google , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-pricing , ai , llms

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.content: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate. ” How Glean uses Jev With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Jev patterns and prototypes Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath , a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks . They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second , even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust ,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts , a Principal Engineer at Workday , finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” Like the early internet The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software . I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an explosion of what software can do, and we will want people to be exploring those boundaries of software. Not necessarily because it's valuable, but because they can, because we have new frontiers to explore , and this is what the early internet was like.”

items.content: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". items.content: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.content: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user. The first is as a safety net — your dot can flag things you may have missed. The second is as “a delegation sink” ; Guo said he uses it “a ton in Slack” for this reason. And the third is as a ubiquitous presence . “I think the third way that dots are a little bit different is we're aiming to make them truly everywhere that you work ,” Guo said. items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.content: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notes Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.content: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter . Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding . As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis . Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: Model Intelligence Index DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 GLM-5.3-Flash: 43 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench . The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card , Naive AI – Research . Model NL2Repo-Bench DeepSWE v1.1 Agent's Last Exam (ALE) GLM-5.3-Flash 56.3 63.4 26.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 68.2 77.0 35.4 Naive-N0.5-Flash 71.9 67.8 32.4 Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed and verbosity experiments Speed is the headline feature. 1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly. 2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500 , 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond . That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. items.content: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.content: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.content: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. items.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.content: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.content: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion . What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project. If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE . You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare. Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it. Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff. Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app. How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer. datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.content: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.content: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett
